comparison: Strong agreement on dose-response electrophysiological findings (C3-C5, C15-C26). Both recognize the reversible, dose-dependent slowing of spontaneous action potentials and selective reduction of diastolic phase. OpenEval emphasizes statistical rigor (Hill fitting, n=6-15), while peer review highlights this as a key strength without methodological critique.

Strong agreement on voltage-clamp findings (C29-C40). Both accept the negative shift of If activation curve and paradoxical voltage-dependent effects. OpenEval details Boltzmann fitting and crossover phenomenon, while peer review emphasizes the cAMP-mediated mechanism as a core strength. Peer review includes C97 (mechanistic conclusion) that OpenEval addresses separately.

Strong agreement on pharmacological controls (C42-C48). Both accept that atropine, DPCPX, and H-89 experiments rule out upstream signaling pathways. OpenEval provides detailed evaluation of statistical comparisons, while peer review implicitly accepts these as supporting the direct channel mechanism without explicit discussion.

Strong agreement on cAMP-dependent antagonism (C50-C55). Both recognize dose-dependent loss of TMYX efficacy with increasing cAMP. OpenEval emphasizes statistical analysis (ANOVA, n=6-15), while peer review focuses on the broader mechanistic conclusion that TMYX antagonizes cAMP-induced modulation. Peer review also includes inside-out patch data (C56-C57, C60-C63) that OpenEval evaluates separately.

Strong agreement on inside-out patch experiments (C56-C63). Both recognize these experiments as key evidence for direct channel interaction and competitive antagonism. OpenEval emphasizes Schild analysis and ki value compatibility, while peer review accepts this as proof that TMYX antagonizes cAMP-induced modulation. Peer review groups this with whole-cell cAMP dose-response data.

Strong agreement on bell-shaped antagonism and physiological implications (C74-C76). Both recognize maximal effect at submaximal cAMP with progressive loss at high cAMP. OpenEval notes C76 lacks direct experimental validation but is mechanistically logical. Peer review explicitly endorses this as a strength, emphasizing therapeutic utility during sympathetic stimulation.

Strong agreement on central mechanistic conclusion (C8, C67, C70, C84, C97). Both accept that TMYX acts as a competitive antagonist of cAMP at the channel level. OpenEval emphasizes convergence of multiple experimental approaches, while peer review lists this as a core strength accepted by all reviewers. Peer review groups this with experimental evidence that OpenEval evaluates separately.

Divergent evaluations of comparative pharmacological claims (C9-C11, C66, C68-C69, C71, C85). OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN, noting lack of direct experimental validation for selective chronotropic action and safety profile. Peer review rates as SUPPORTED, accepting the comparison to β-blockers/muscarinic antagonists as valid and emphasizing therapeutic utility. This represents a key difference in evidentiary standards.

Partial agreement on therapeutic implications (C104-C109). OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED but notes comparisons with ivabradine lack head-to-head experiments and clinical safety claims are speculative. Peer review rates therapeutic potential (C77, C85, C103, C108) as SUPPORTED, with editor and reviewers endorsing high therapeutic utility. Both acknowledge limitations but differ in confidence level.

Agreement on speculative nature of clinical applications (C77, C82, C103). OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN, noting lack of clinical efficacy data and reliance on analogy. Peer review groups these with therapeutic implications rated as SUPPORTED, though acknowledges lack of robust clinical data. Both recognize these as hypotheses requiring future validation.

Agreement that TMYX complexity is a limitation (C86-C88, C135). OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED, accepting the inference of single active component from unified dose-response behavior while noting synergistic effects cannot be excluded. Peer review rates as UNCERTAIN, with reviewers explicitly requesting identification of active ingredients as an important next step. Both recognize this as a gap requiring future work.

Strong agreement on background context (C1-C2, C89-C93). Both accept these claims as appropriate background establishing the knowledge gap and clinical context. OpenEval notes these come from cited literature rather than original data. Peer review accepts this background as valid motivation for the study.

Strong agreement on HCN channel pharmacology context (C64-C65, C78, C133-C134). Both accept these literature-based comparisons as valid contextualization. OpenEval emphasizes they provide perspective on cAMP-binding domain modulation. Peer review accepts these as established knowledge supporting TMYX's mechanism without challenge.

Divergent evaluations of PDE/microdomain discussion (C116-C123). OpenEval rates background claims as SUPPORTED, accepting them as established knowledge appropriately cited. Peer review rates as UNCERTAIN, with Reviewer #1 explicitly requesting expanded discussion of PDEs and microdomain cAMP signaling, questioning whether TMYX acts via PDE2. This indicates peer review found the treatment insufficient.

OpenEval evaluated ethical compliance and material sourcing claims (C136-C138) as SUPPORTED standard methodological statements. No corresponding peer review evaluation found, though R7 shares C138. These administrative claims were not explicitly discussed by peer reviewers.
